title: How Your Writing Is Marked
summary: The five writing categories (25 marks) explained in plain English, what top marks need in each, the rules that cap marks, and the G.A.A.P. and G.C.S.P.P. planning techniques with a 35-minute plan and checking routine.

blocks.text: Section B of each paper is worth **25 marks** — half the paper. The examiner does not give one overall impression mark. Instead, your writing is marked against **five separate categories**, and the marks are added together. When you know exactly what each category rewards, you can write to collect every mark. This page explains the categories, the special rules that limit marks, and the two planning techniques used throughout this course: **G.A.A.P.** for Paper 1 and **G.C.S.P.P.** for Paper 2.
The five categories at a glance
The same five categories are used for Paper 1 (non-fiction) and Paper 2 (fiction), and for both the Stage 8 Progression Test and Checkpoint 0861.

rows: Creation of texts
Wc
Is your content relevant, developed and right for the text type, purpose and reader?
Vocabulary and language
Wv
Did you choose words carefully and for effect?
Structure of texts (Text structure)
Ws
Is the whole piece well organised, paragraphed and linked?
Grammar and punctuation (Sentence structure, punctuation and grammar)
Wg
Are your sentences accurate, varied and punctuated well — and used for effect?
Word structure (spelling)
Ww
Can you spell accurately, including ambitious words?
Total

blocks.text: Look at the numbers. **Structure (7) and Grammar and punctuation (7) together are worth 14 marks — more than half.** A well-organised piece with varied, accurate sentences will always score well, even if the ideas are simple. Creation of texts (5) is almost as valuable as Vocabulary and Spelling put together (3 + 3 = 6), so content and text type matter a lot too.

blocks.title: How the examiner uses the bands
blocks.text: Each category has bands (for example 1, 2–3, 4–5, 6–7). The examiner starts at the lowest band and moves up while your writing meets the description: this is called **best fit**. If you meet only some of a band's description, you get the lower mark in that band. If you do not meet even the lowest description, that category scores 0. So the aim is to show **every** feature of the top band clearly, not just one or two.
Special rules that limit your mark

rows: Very short answer
20 words or fewer = **0 marks in total**. 21–60 words = **maximum 7 marks in total**.
Sixty words is only about eight handwritten lines. Aim for 350+ words.
Wrong text type
If you write the wrong kind of text (e.g. a story instead of an article), Creation of texts is capped at **1**, and Structure is also capped (at about 3, or lower if the content is also off-task).
Underline the text type in the task. Use its layout features from the first line.
Planning
The planning space is **not marked**.
Plan in notes, not sentences. Spend 4–5 minutes, no more.
Punctuation errors
Good English is not punished heavily for a few punctuation slips, but if punctuation is almost absent you get the lower mark.
Full stops and capitals first. Then add commas, apostrophes and a wider range.

blocks.text: 1. Creation of texts (Wc) — 5 marks
This category is about **content and purpose**: does your writing answer the actual task, does it read like the text type you were asked for, and does it keep the reader in mind from start to finish?

rows: Some content linked to the topic with a little development, or a few recognisable features of the text type. Wrong text type = this band at most.
Content is partly relevant. Features of the text type appear here and there, not consistently. A simple viewpoint that mostly fits the purpose.
Content is mostly relevant with a range of developed ideas. Features of the text type are used throughout. The viewpoint is consistent, and the writer's own style starts to show.

Content is fully relevant and well developed, with specific details. A wide range of text-type features is used successfully. The writer keeps a clear relationship with the reader all the way through and sustains interest.

blocks.title: How to get 5/5 in Creation of texts
items: Cover **every** point or bullet in the task — and develop each one with details, examples and explanation, not one line each.
Use the features of the text type **throughout**, not only in the opening (e.g. a persuasive article keeps using direct address, rhetorical questions and emotive language to the end).
Keep one clear viewpoint or narrative voice. Do not change your opinion or your narrator half-way.
Talk to your reader: in non-fiction, remind them why it matters to them. In fiction, keep them curious about what happens next.
Be specific. 'A small café by the harbour that smelt of cardamom' is worth more than 'a nice place'.

blocks.text: 2. Vocabulary and language (Wv) — 3 marks
This category rewards **word choice**. Correct words are not enough for the top band: your words must be chosen for an effect — to persuade, to describe, to create a mood or to sound expert.

rows: Vocabulary is correct and on topic, but plain.
Vocabulary suits the text type, with some descriptive, emotive or topic-specific words. The tone fits the purpose.
Ambitious, specialised vocabulary is used well across the whole piece, clearly chosen for effect and to create the right mood or tone.
The market was busy and loud.
The market heaved with shoppers, and the air rang with the cries of traders.
Plastic is bad for the sea.
Discarded plastic is quietly choking our coastline.
He was scared.
His stomach tightened, and a cold dread crept up his spine.
The film was good.
The film is gripping from its first scene to its final, unexpected twist.

blocks.title: How to get 3/3 in Vocabulary
items: Learn 10–15 topic words for each genre pack in this course and use several in every piece.
Replace weak words: good, bad, nice, big, very, a lot, thing, stuff, said, went.
Choose verbs with power (crept, seized, soared) — strong verbs often do more than adjectives.
Match the register: formal words for a report or formal letter, warm and lively words for a blog or story.
Keep it up to the end. Many students use their best words in the first paragraph and then stop.

blocks.text: 3. Structure of texts (Ws) — 7 marks
This category looks at the **whole piece**: the opening, the order of ideas, the paragraphs, the links between them, and the ending.

rows: Separate points can be seen. Very basic organisation.
Related ideas are grouped. Some logical order, with simple connectives (and, also, because, then). There may be an opening and/or ending.
Ideas develop logically through the whole piece. **Paragraphs are used properly** and linked so the writing flows.
Well-organised paragraphs, clearly linked within and between paragraphs with a wide range of connectives, building to an effective whole with a strong opening and ending.

blocks.title: How to get 7/7 in Structure
items: Plan the order before you write: opening → 2–4 developed body paragraphs → ending.
One main idea per paragraph. Start each with a topic sentence (non-fiction) or a change of time, place or action (fiction).
Link paragraphs: use connectives (Furthermore, However, As a result, Later that evening, By the time…) or echo a word from the previous paragraph.
Make the opening hook the reader and the ending complete the piece (a call to action, a recommendation, a reflection, a resolution or a twist).
In stories, vary the pace: a one-line paragraph at the moment of tension can be very effective.

blocks.text: 4. Grammar and punctuation (Wg) — 7 marks
This category looks at your **sentences**: their accuracy, their variety and whether you use them **for effect**. It also checks punctuation — accurate basics first, then a wider range.

rows: Simple sentences mostly correct. Full stops and capital letters mostly accurate.
Simple and compound sentences, with some attempts at complex ones. Verb tenses usually consistent. Basic punctuation mostly correct.

Grammar accurate almost throughout. A confident mix of simple, compound and complex sentences. Expanded noun phrases. Correct verb forms and modal verbs. Commas used correctly, including to mark clauses.

Sentence types and lengths are chosen deliberately for effect. Clauses are reordered for emphasis. A wide range of punctuation (e.g. colons, semicolons, dashes, brackets) is used accurately and with purpose.

blocks.title: How to get 7/7 in Grammar and punctuation
items: Use all four sentence types: simple, compound, complex and compound-complex — and place a **short sentence** where you want impact.
Open some sentences with a subordinate clause ('Although the rain had stopped, …'), a fronted adverbial ('Without warning, …') or an -ing/-ed phrase ('Exhausted from the climb, …').
Use at least one each of: a colon (to introduce a list or explanation), a semicolon (to join two related main clauses), a pair of dashes or brackets (for extra information), and accurate apostrophes.
Keep your tense consistent: past for stories and recounts, present for reviews and most articles.
Use modal verbs in non-fiction for force or politeness: must, should, could, might.

blocks.text: Examples of sentence-level effects you can copy:

items: **Short sentence for impact:** 'For three weeks, we had trained every evening on the dusty pitch behind the school. Then the storm came.'
**Reordered clause for emphasis:** 'Because every bottle we throw away lasts for centuries, we must act today.'
**Colon for explanation:** 'The answer was simple: we needed more volunteers.'
**Semicolon joining two related sentences:** 'The old lighthouse stood empty; nobody had climbed its stairs for years.'
**Pair of dashes for extra information:** 'My grandfather — who had never left his village before — gripped the railing of the ferry.'

blocks.text: 5. Word structure (spelling) (Ww) — 3 marks
This category is about **spelling**, from everyday words to ambitious ones.

rows: Common and high-frequency words, regular plurals and common prefixes and suffixes are mostly correct.
Words with double consonants, silent letters, common exception words and a wider range of prefixes and suffixes are mostly correct.
Ambitious and topic-specific words, commonly misspelt words, tricky endings and easily confused homophones are spelt correctly.
Commonly misspelt
necessary, definitely, separate, environment, recommend, beginning, believe, government, embarrassed, accommodation
Double consonants
stopped, travelling (British), occurred, beginning, committee, address
Silent letters
knowledge, island, doubt, rhythm, muscle, wrist
Tricky endings
-tion/-cian (information, musician) · -able/-ible (comfortable, responsible) · -ance/-ence (appearance, independence)
Homophones
their/there/they're · your/you're · aloud/allowed · whether/weather · affect/effect · desert/dessert · practise (verb)/practice (noun)

blocks.title: How to get 3/3 in Spelling
items: Use British spelling consistently: colour, favourite, organise, centre, travelled.
Learn the spelling of every vocabulary word you plan to use — an ambitious word spelt wrongly loses its value.
Save three minutes at the end to check homophones and the words you know you often get wrong.

blocks.title: أهم 5 نصائح للدرجة النهائية في الكتابة
items: اكتب نفس نوع النص المطلوب بالضبط (مقال، رسالة، قصة...)؛ لو كتبت نوعًا آخر تخسر معظم الدرجات حتى لو لغتك ممتازة.
غطِّ كل النقاط المطلوبة في السؤال واشرح كل نقطة بالتفصيل والأمثلة.
التنظيم والقواعد عليهما 14 درجة من 25: فقرات واضحة، روابط متنوعة، وأنواع جمل مختلفة.
استخدم علامات ترقيم متنوعة وصحيحة: النقطتان (:) والفاصلة المنقوطة (;) والشرطتان (– –).
لا تكتب أقل من 60 كلمة أبدًا؛ الهدف 350 كلمة أو أكثر، واترك 3 دقائق لمراجعة الإملاء.

blocks.text: Paper 1: the G.A.A.P. technique

Before you write a single sentence of a non-fiction answer, spend the first few minutes breaking the task down with **G.A.A.P.** Each letter is a decision you must make, and each one is linked to marks.

rows: **G — Genre**
What **layout** (text type) is it: article, review, letter, email, report, speech, diary? And what exact **topic**?
Headline, greeting, sub-headings, sign-off. Staying precisely on the topic (not 'the environment' in general if the task says 'litter in the park').
Creation of texts and Structure (wrong text type caps both)
**A — Audience**
Who will read it, and where? A school magazine for students? A letter to a head teacher? The local council?
Register: formal or informal, how you address the reader, the vocabulary you choose.
Vocabulary and language, Creation of texts
**A — Area of content**
What points does the task tell me to include?
Underline every point. Use **all** of them and develop each in its own paragraph.
Creation of texts (relevance and development)
**P — Purpose**
Is it to inform, explain, describe, recount, argue, persuade or review?
The toolkit: e.g. persuade → rhetorical questions, direct address, emotive words, call to action. Inform → clear facts, neutral tone, sub-headings.
Creation of texts, Vocabulary

blocks.text: **Worked example.** Task: *Your school website is running a feature called 'Our City, Our Future'. Write an article encouraging students to use public transport, cycle or walk to school. You should explain the problems caused by so many car journeys, what students can do, and how the school could help.*

rows: Genre — layout
Article: headline, strong opening, 3–4 paragraphs, possibly sub-headings, a closing call to action.
Genre — topic
Getting to school without a car — not pollution in general.
Audience
Students at my school reading the website → semi-formal, lively, 'we' and 'you', no slang.
Area of content

(1) problems caused by car journeys (traffic at the gate, pollution, lack of exercise). (2) what students can do (walk in groups, cycle, school bus). (3) how the school could help (bike racks, safe crossing, a 'Walk on Wednesday' challenge).
Purpose
Persuade + inform → rhetorical questions, statistics-style facts, emotive language, modal verbs (must, could), call to action.

blocks.title: G.A.A.P. in the exam
blocks.text: Write G, A, A, P down the side of the planning space and fill each line in a few words. This takes 2–3 minutes and stops the three biggest mistakes: wrong text type, wrong tone and a missing bullet point.
Paper 2: the G.C.S.P.P. technique
For a story, make every big decision **before** you write, so you do not change direction half-way. Use **G.C.S.P.P.**

rows: **G — Genre**
What kind of story suits the task: realistic, adventure, mystery, horror, fantasy, science fiction?
Genre sets the mood, vocabulary and atmosphere (e.g. mystery → clues and questions, adventure → risk, movement and a goal).
**C — Characters**
Who is in the story, what is each one's role, and how are they related?
Keep it to 2–4 characters. Know your main character's personality and what he or she wants.
**S — Setting**
Where and when does it happen? Is the setting given in the task?
If the setting is given, use it and stay consistent. If not, choose one that fits the genre and helps the mood.
**P — Point of view**
First person ('I') or third person ('he/she')?
First person feels personal; third person lets you describe more. If you continue a given story, keep its point of view exactly.
**P — Plot**
Which part am I writing: a complete story, an opening, an ending or a continuation?
For a complete story: opening → build-up → problem/climax → resolution. Follow every bullet prompt in the task.

blocks.text: **Worked example.** Task: *Write a story about someone who has to finish an important task before time runs out. You should describe the setting, the main character and what happens.*

rows: Genre
Realistic fiction with suspense.
Characters
Yassin (14, careful, worried about letting people down) · his younger sister Salma · Mr Hany, the bakery owner.
Setting
A small family bakery in Alexandria at dawn on the morning of a wedding; the oven has broken.
Point of view
Third person, past tense, close to Yassin's thoughts.
Plot

Complete story: (1) dawn, smell of bread, order for 200 pastries. (2) the oven dies. (3) race across the city to borrow a neighbour's oven, with the clock ticking. (4) the last tray arrives as the wedding begins. (5) Yassin realises he is calmer under pressure than he thought.

blocks.title: Continuation tasks
blocks.text: If a task asks you to continue the story from the extract, re-read the extract first and lock in the characters, setting, point of view and tone. Your continuation must feel like the same story — same names, same personalities, same narrator. Switching from 'I' to 'he' is a serious and avoidable error.
Using your 35 minutes
Most Year 8 students can produce **350–450 words** of careful writing in 35 minutes with this plan:

rows: 0–4 min
Decode and plan

Underline the text type, audience, purpose and every bullet. Fill in G.A.A.P. or G.C.S.P.P. in notes. Write a 4–5 line paragraph plan, and jot 5–6 strong words and one or two punctuation features you will use.
4–8 min
Opening
Write the headline/greeting (non-fiction) or a hooking first line (fiction), then the opening paragraph.
8–28 min
Body
One paragraph per point or story stage, about 5 minutes each. Link every paragraph. Check you are covering every bullet.
Ending
A clear conclusion: call to action, recommendation, reflection, or a satisfying resolution.
Check
Run the checking routine below. Correct neatly with a single line through any mistake.

blocks.text: A planning frame you can copy
Draw this quickly in the planning space. It works for both papers.

rows: Technique
Opening
Headline + hook (question, surprising fact, short scene)
Hook: action, dialogue, setting or a question
Paragraph 2
Bullet point 1 + details/example
Build-up: characters and setting described
Paragraph 3
Bullet point 2 + details/example
The problem appears
Paragraph 4
Bullet point 3 + details/example (or counter-argument)
Climax: tension at its highest
Ending
Call to action / recommendation / reflection
Resolution + how the character has changed
Toolkit
6 strong words · 1 colon · 1 semicolon · 1 pair of dashes · 1 rhetorical question
6 strong words · 1 simile/metaphor · 1 short sentence · 1 fronted adverbial · speech punctuated correctly

blocks.text: The 3-minute checking routine

items: **Task:** Have I written the right text type and covered every bullet point?
**Paragraphs:** Is there a clear opening, body and ending, with each paragraph linked?
**Sentences:** Is there at least one simple, one compound and one complex sentence, and a short sentence for effect?
**Punctuation:** Full stops and capitals · commas after opening clauses · apostrophes (it's/its) · speech marks in stories · my planned colon, semicolon and dashes.
**Tense:** Have I stayed in the same tense?
**Spelling:** Check homophones (their/there, your/you're, whether/weather) and every ambitious word.

blocks.text: Common mistakes that cost writing marks

rows: Writing a story when the task asks for an article, or a letter without a greeting
Creation of texts, Structure
Use G.A.A.P. and put the layout features in first.
Missing one of the bullet points
Creation of texts
Tick each bullet in the plan as you write it.
One long paragraph
Structure (cannot pass band 2–3)
New paragraph for each new point, time, place, speaker or event.
Every sentence starts with 'I' or 'Then'
Grammar and punctuation, Structure
Vary openings: adverbials, -ing phrases, subordinate clauses.
Comma splices: 'It was late, we went home.'
Grammar and punctuation
Use a full stop, a semicolon, or a conjunction.
Changing tense in the middle of a story
Grammar and punctuation
Decide on past tense and check it at the end.
Strong words only in the first paragraph
Vocabulary
Spread your planned words across the whole piece.
Running out of time with no ending
Structure
Watch the clock. Start the ending at minute 28 at the latest.

blocks.title: خطة الـ35 دقيقة في الكتابة
blocks.text: أول 4 دقائق: اقرأ السؤال وحدد نوع النص والقارئ والهدف وكل النقاط المطلوبة باستخدام G.A.A.P. في الورقة الأولى أو G.C.S.P.P. في القصة، واكتب خطة سريعة في كلمات وليس جملًا. من الدقيقة 4 إلى 28: اكتب المقدمة ثم فقرة لكل نقطة. من 28 إلى 32: الخاتمة. آخر 3 دقائق: راجع الفقرات وعلامات الترقيم والأزمنة والإملاء. الخطة نفسها لا تُصحح، لكنها تحميك من أكبر الأخطاء.
Practice: decode these tasks
For each task, write a G.A.A.P. or G.C.S.P.P. breakdown before you look at the answer.

items.q: Paper 1 task: 'Your town's youth centre may close. Write a letter to the local council explaining what the centre offers young people, why it matters, and what could be done to keep it open.' — Break it down with G.A.A.P.
items.a: G (layout): formal letter — addresses, date, 'Dear Sir or Madam,', paragraphs, 'Yours faithfully,' + full name. G (topic): keeping the youth centre open. A (audience): council officials → formal, polite, no contractions. A (area of content): (1) what the centre offers. (2) why it matters to young people. (3) ways to keep it open (volunteers, fundraising, shared use). P (purpose): persuade + explain → reasons with examples, modal verbs (should, could), a polite but firm request at the end.

items.q: Paper 1 task: 'Write a review of a place to eat in your area for a website read by families. Describe the place, the food and the service, and say who you would recommend it to.' — Break it down with G.A.A.P.
items.a: G (layout): review — title naming the place, star rating (optional), opening that sets the scene, a paragraph each on place, food, service, and a recommendation. G (topic): one specific local restaurant or café. A (audience): parents and families online → friendly, semi-formal, helpful. A (area of content): description of the place · the food · the service · who it suits. P (purpose): inform + give opinion → descriptive vocabulary, balanced positives and a negative, a clear final verdict.

items.q: Paper 2 task: 'Write a story about a character who discovers that a place they know well is hiding a secret.' — Break it down with G.C.S.P.P.
items.a: G: mystery. C: Nour (13, curious, observant) and her grandfather, plus perhaps one minor character (the caretaker). S: grandfather's old flat in a quiet Cairo street, with a locked cupboard behind the bookcase. P (point of view): first person, past tense, to share Nour's curiosity. P (plot): complete story — normal visit → strange detail noticed → search and tension → the secret revealed (old letters showing the grandfather's past) → what Nour now understands about him.

items.q: Paper 2 task: 'Continue the story from the extract, describing what happens when the storm reaches the village.' The extract is told in third person about a fisherman named Karim. What two things must you NOT change, and why?
items.a: You must keep the third-person point of view and keep Karim's character (name, personality, relationships) and the village setting exactly as in the extract. A continuation is marked on how naturally it follows the original. Switching to 'I' or changing who Karim is would be a serious consistency error and would weaken Creation of texts and Structure.

items.q: A student wrote 55 excellent words before running out of time. What is the highest writing mark possible, and what lesson does this teach?
items.a: The maximum is 7 out of 25, because answers of 21–60 words are capped at 7. Lesson: manage your time — reading must stop at about 35 minutes so that you have enough time to write a full answer.

items.q: Which category is worth more: Vocabulary and language plus Word structure (spelling) together, or Creation of texts on its own?
items.a: Vocabulary (3) + Spelling (3) = 6, while Creation of texts = 5, so Vocabulary and Spelling together are worth one mark more. But notice that Creation of texts alone is almost as valuable as both of them, and the two biggest categories are Structure (7) and Grammar and punctuation (7).
